answer.label: Not Virginia Woolf — an anonymous 2024 internet passage
answer.sourceLine: No Woolf work contains this line. The earliest known appearance is a Facebook post dated 26 August 2024, which credited it to To the Lighthouse, but the line isn’t in that novel. Snopes ↗ rated the attribution “Unproven.” The Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain ↗ found it in none of her works and called it “Possibly designed by AI.”

source.heading: Where the passage actually comes from

docMeta.dd: No. Absent from her novels, essays, Diary and Letters
To the Lighthouse (1927), which does not contain it
Snopes: “Unproven” (30 Oct 2024); VWSGB: “Possibly designed by AI”

source.excerpt: There is a kind of sadness that comes from knowing too much, from seeing the world as it truly is. It is the sadness of understanding that life is not a grand adventure, but a series of small, insignificant moments, that love is not a fairy tale, but a fragile, fleeting emotion, that happiness is not a permanent state, but a rare, fleeting glimpse of something we can never hold onto. And in that understanding, there is a profound loneliness, a sense of being cut off from the world, from other people, from oneself.
trail: Snopes, 30 October 2024 ↗: the earliest securely datable post is from 26 August 2024, on the Facebook page Philosophy Insights, which credited To the Lighthouse. Snopes found the passage nowhere in that novel, the Delphi Complete Works, the five volumes of the Diary or the six volumes of the Letters. Rating: “Unproven.”

Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain ↗: “none of the phrases, nor the quotation as a whole, appear in any of Woolf’s works.” Its verdict on the source is “Possibly designed by AI,” and it dates the first online mention to a Facebook ‘philosophy’ page post of 26 August 2024.
Wikiquote’s Virginia Woolf page ↗ does not include the line, and it sends readers to the Virginia Woolf Society’s misquotations page for misattributions it doesn’t list.
source.excerptNote: This is the full passage as it spreads on social media, in the wording that Snopes and the Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain transcribe. The usual quote is its first sentence. Neither the sentence nor the passage appears in any of Woolf’s works.

author.name: Virginia Woolf
author.heading: About Virginia Woolf
author.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English modernist writer and one of the most influential twentieth-century authors. She wrote Mrs Dalloway, To the Lighthouse and A Room of One’s Own. She did not write this passage: it first surfaced online in 2024, and her author society lists it among the misquotations pinned to her.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented: post by the Facebook page Philosophy Insights, 26 August 2024, attributing the passage to Virginia Woolf’s To the Lighthouse (where it does not appear). Reported in Caroline Wazer, “Virginia Woolf Said, ‘There Is a Kind of Sadness That Comes from Knowing Too Much’?” Snopes, October 30, 2024 (updated November 4, 2024); see also Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain, “Misquotations and Misattributions.”

misattribution.heading: How a 2024 post became “Virginia Woolf”
misattribution.intro: The passage spread across Facebook, X and Instagram in August and September 2024 with Woolf’s name on it. Sometimes a specific novel was named, but usually no work was cited at all.

items.why: The earliest securely datable post, by the Facebook page Philosophy Insights, named this novel. Snopes ↗ searched a HathiTrust copy: the word “sadness” appears twice, and neither instance resembles the quote.
The Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain ↗ notes the passage is credited to Woolf “but not to a specific work – always a warning sign!” It says the lines “sound very unlike Woolf.”

Snopes ↗ reports that the AI detectors Quillbot, ZeroGPT and Merlin rated the passage likely AI-generated. The VWSGB ↗ gives its source as “Possibly designed by AI.” Neither claims to have identified a specific author.

misattribution.truthLine: Woolf didn’t write it. The passage first appears online on 26 August 2024, and per the Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain ↗ it is absent from all of her works.

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: The passage has a lot of melancholy and very little content: life is “a series of small, insignificant moments,” love “a fragile, fleeting emotion.” Pinned to a writer known for her inner life and her depression, it read as authentic to many readers. Snopes found one Facebook post that drew around 16,000 reactions, with commenters taking the attribution at face value.

Snopes stopped at “Unproven” because it couldn’t rule out an unpublished manuscript or a remark someone recorded in conversation. Woolf’s own author society went further after its investigation, finding the passage in none of her works and suggesting it was machine-made.
detailsBody: Snopes searched To the Lighthouse (HathiTrust), the Delphi Complete Works of Virginia Woolf, the five volumes of The Diary of Virginia Woolf and the six volumes of The Letters of Virginia Woolf, and found the passage in none of them. It updated its article on 4 November 2024 to add the Virginia Woolf Society’s findings.
The pull-quote above is the Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain’s own judgment of the passage, not a line by Woolf.
context.pull: The lines sound very unlike Woolf, who would have stated her point much more succinctly.
